docs.title: AI & Engineering Strategy on a Page (PDF)
docs.tl_dr: One-page summary of the AI and engineering strategy: embed Claude into development workflows (GitHub Copilot, IDE integration), launch a test automation platform, and establish governance. Directs product and engineering teams on investment priorities. Locks in a 12-month roadmap.

faqs.q: What's the main goal of this strategy?
faqs.a: Scale AI adoption across engineering by making Claude available in the tools developers use daily (IDE, GitHub, test frameworks) while maintaining governance and security.

faqs.q: What are the three pillars?
faqs.a: Tooling Integration (Copilot, IDE plugins), Test Automation (intelligent test platform), and Governance (SDLC 2.0 framework).

faqs.q: When is GitHub Copilot rolling out?
faqs.a: Phase 1: Q2 2024 (early access, 50 users). Phase 2: Q3 2024 (full rollout, all engineers).

faqs.q: What's the test automation play?
faqs.a: Build a platform that uses Claude to generate, optimize, and maintain test suites. Pilot on one product; measure velocity and coverage improvements.

faqs.q: Who funds this?
faqs.a: Engineering budget + vendor relationships. GitHub Copilot cost is ~$3K/month for initial seats. Test platform is internal build.

faqs.q: What's the success metric?
faqs.a: 30% reduction in test maintenance time and 25% faster feature velocity by end of 12 months.

docs.title: SDLC 2.0 Staff One-Pager
docs.tl_dr: Quick reference guide to SDLC 2.0 for all staff: explains the three tiers, what's required of you, and how to get approval. Single page; use it to fast-track your AI project through intake. Commits everyone to submitting AI work through the formal process.

faqs.q: What's SDLC 2.0 in one sentence?
faqs.a: It's the organization's process for safely and securely building with AI, with three tiers of governance depending on how risky your project is.

faqs.q: Which tier am I in?
faqs.a: Tier 1 (low-risk): Internal experiments, no revenue impact. Tier 2 (medium-risk): Production-adjacent, affects customers indirectly. Tier 3 (high-risk): Direct customer impact, regulated, or high cost of failure. Use the intake form to determine.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to start?
faqs.a: All projects must be submitted via the AI Use Case Intake Form. Tier-1 gets auto-approved; Tier-2 needs AI Council review; Tier-3 needs Council + legal + board.

faqs.q: How do I submit my project?
faqs.a: Complete the AI Use Case Intake Form (on the Intelligence Hub) and email to [governance contact]. Expect Tier-1 approval in 2 days, Tier-2 in 5 days, Tier-3 in 10 days.

faqs.q: What controls do I have to implement?
faqs.a: Tier-1: Basic data tagging, unit tests, incident escalation. Tier-2: Add model drift monitoring and quarterly security review. Tier-3: Full control set including legal review and red-team testing.

faqs.q: Can I start before approval?
faqs.a: Tier-1 projects can start scoping; no code or data work until approved. Tier-2 and Tier-3 must wait for full approval before any engineering.

docs.title: SDLC 2.0 Strategy — Embedding Claude across the Lifecycle
docs.tl_dr: Defines how Claude integrates across the AI/ML lifecycle—from intake through monitoring—with a three-tier governance model and controls mapped to regulatory domains. Targets engineering leadership and risk teams deciding on AI investment and control maturity. Commits the organization to embedding Claude-native security, testing, and review at each lifecycle stage.

faqs.q: What is SDLC 2.0 and who should use this document?
faqs.a: SDLC 2.0 is the organization's strategy for embedding Claude across the AI/ML development lifecycle. Use this if you're evaluating AI use cases, designing governance, or deciding which controls to implement. It's for engineering leadership, product teams, and risk.

faqs.q: What are the three tiers in the SDLC 2.0 model?
faqs.a: Tier 1 (Low-risk): Low-value experiments, minimal control overhead. Tier 2 (Medium-risk): Production-adjacent, requires Council review. Tier 3 (High-risk): Regulated or revenue-critical, needs full governance, legal review, and board-level sign-off.

faqs.q: Do I need Council approval for a Tier-2 use case?
faqs.a: Yes. All Tier-2 use cases require AI Council review and documented decision. Tier-1 projects are exempt. Tier-3 projects need Council approval plus legal and board escalation.

faqs.q: What control domains are covered?
faqs.a: Nine control domains: Data Governance, Model Governance, Testing & QA, Security & Privacy, Monitoring & Incident Response, Ethical Use, Change Management, Third-Party Risk, and Audit & Compliance.

faqs.q: What happens if a use case moves between tiers?
faqs.a: Re-submit for Council review at the higher tier. If it moves to Tier-3, escalate to legal and board. Document the reclassification and trigger appropriate governance controls.

faqs.q: How often is SDLC 2.0 reviewed?
faqs.a: Annually or when material changes occur (e.g., new regulatory requirements, critical incident, technology shifts). Review is owned by the Head of AI & Automation in consultation with the AI Council.

faqs.q: What's the relationship between SDLC 2.0 and the Control Register?
faqs.a: SDLC 2.0 defines the overall governance strategy and tier framework. The Control Register (separate doc) lists the specific 40+ controls mapped to each domain and how they map to regulatory requirements.

faqs.q: Can I skip controls for a Tier-1 project?
faqs.a: No. Even Tier-1 projects require baseline controls: data classification, basic testing, and incident escalation. Tier-1 exemption only applies to Council review, not to control implementation.

faqs.q: Who owns the SDLC 2.0 governance day-to-day?
faqs.a: Head of AI & Automation owns policy and framework updates. The AI Council approves tier classifications. Engineering teams implement controls. Risk & Compliance audit adherence.

faqs.q: How is this document related to the AI Council Charter?
faqs.a: SDLC 2.0 is the framework; the AI Council Charter defines who reviews decisions, how they vote, and what escalations trigger. Together they form the governance operating model.

docs.title: AI Acceptable Use Policy
docs.tl_dr: Prohibited and allowed uses of Claude and AI tools: no PII without encryption, no financial account numbers, no copyrighted training data, no unreviewed regulatory submissions. Covers confidentiality, audit rights, and user training. Applies to all employees and contractors.

faqs.q: Can I feed customer data to Claude?
faqs.a: Only if: 1) it's classified as internal use; 2) encrypted in transit; 3) retention is set to 30 days; 4) documented in your use case intake. PII is prohibited without legal review.

faqs.q: Can I use Claude to write code from copyrighted open-source?
faqs.a: No. Don't train Claude on proprietary or copyrighted code. Fair use in specific contexts (code review, analysis) may be OK; check with legal first.

faqs.q: What's prohibited?
faqs.a: Financial account numbers, passwords, API keys, medical records, unencrypted PII, regulatory submissions without review, external data sharing, reverse-engineering IP.

faqs.q: Can I export Claude responses for use in production?
faqs.a: Yes, if: 1) use case is approved (Tier-1+); 2) outputs are reviewed by a human; 3) responsibility is documented (who owns the output).

faqs.q: Who audits compliance with this policy?
faqs.a: Risk & Compliance team (quarterly). Violations reported to CTO. Repeat violations trigger disciplinary review.

faqs.q: Is there training required?
faqs.a: Yes. All staff complete onboarding training (20 mins). Annual refresher required. Engineering teams get deep dive (2 hours).

faqs.q: What happens if I accidentally breach the policy?
faqs.a: Report to Head of AI & Automation within 24h. Immediate notification and assessment of impact. No disciplinary action if self-reported promptly.

faqs.q: Can I use Claude for hiring decisions?
faqs.a: No. Do not feed candidate data or use Claude outputs for hiring decisions. HR retains all responsibility and bias review.

faqs.q: Does this policy apply to contractors?
faqs.a: Yes. Contractors must sign attestation in their SOW. Violations handled same as employees.

docs.title: AI Council Charter & Decision Log
docs.tl_dr: Charter sets Council membership, voting rules, decision-log format, and meeting cadence. Monthly decision log tracks tier classifications, approvals, and key discussions. Ensures transparent, auditable governance. Commits Council to weekly meetings during active cycles.

faqs.q: What is the AI Council?
faqs.a: A 5-person committee (Head of AI & Automation, CTO, CRO, CLO, Head of Product) that reviews Tier-2 and Tier-3 use cases and makes tier classification/approval decisions.

faqs.q: How often does the Council meet?
faqs.a: Weekly during active governance cycles (intake coming in). Ad-hoc otherwise. Meetings are 1 hour. Decisions logged and published within 24h.

faqs.q: What's the voting rule?
faqs.a: Majority (3 of 5) required for Tier-2 approval. Tier-3 requires unanimous Council + legal/board sign-off. Chair (Head of AI & Automation) breaks ties.

faqs.q: Can someone delegate their Council seat?
faqs.a: No. Only the named member or their direct report (with prior Council agreement) can vote. Attendance is required.

faqs.q: What's in the decision log?
faqs.a: Date, project name, tier, decision (approved/deferred/rejected), vote count, rationale, action items, owner. Published to all staff monthly.

faqs.q: How do I request a reconsideration if my Tier-2 is rejected?
faqs.a: Address Council feedback (in the decision log) and resubmit with updated materials. Can resubmit next meeting cycle. No appeal process; Council decision is final.

faqs.q: Are Council meetings public?
faqs.a: Meetings are private. Decision log is public. Staff can request materials review if their project was discussed.

faqs.q: Who manages Council logistics?
faqs.a: Governance analyst (new hire in Q2). Books meetings, distributes agendas, records decisions, publishes log.

faqs.q: When is the first Council meeting?
faqs.a: Week 5 of 90-day plan (after Charter is board-approved). Schedule TBD.

docs.title: AI Governance Framework
docs.tl_dr: Governance operating model: defines roles (Council, review committee, teams), decision rights (tiering, escalation paths), and control areas (data, model, security, incident). Applies to all Claude use cases. Commits organization to formal AI oversight.

faqs.q: What is the AI Governance Framework and who needs to read it?
faqs.a: It's the rulebook for how AI decisions are made, who approves what, and how we manage risk. Read it if you're launching an AI project or are part of governance (Council, engineering leadership, risk).

faqs.q: What's the decision hierarchy?
faqs.a: Tier-1: Auto-approved after intake. Tier-2: AI Council vote (3 of 5 must approve). Tier-3: Council + legal + board. Escalations go to CTO if Council deadlocked.

faqs.q: Who sits on the AI Council?
faqs.a: Head of AI & Automation (Chair), CTO, Chief Risk Officer, Chief Legal Officer, Head of Product. Quorum = 3 (including Chair). Meets weekly during active governance cycle.

faqs.q: What are the control areas?
faqs.a: Data (classification, lineage, access); Model (versioning, drift, retraining); Security (encryption, access, audit); Testing (coverage, drift detection); Incident (detection, response, post-mortem).

faqs.q: How do I escalate an issue?
faqs.a: Severity 1 (data breach, model hijack, major outage): immediate verbal to CTO, then Council. Severity 2 (drift detected, minor incident): email to Head of AI within 24h. Severity 3 (operational blocker): weekly sync.

faqs.q: What's the approval SLA?
faqs.a: Tier-1: 2 days (auto). Tier-2: 5 days (Council meeting + vote). Tier-3: 10 days (Council + legal + board scheduling).

faqs.q: Do I need re-approval if my use case changes?
faqs.a: Material change (e.g., scope increases, moves to production): yes, resubmit. Minor tweak (bug fix, small feature): no, notify Head of AI & Automation.

faqs.q: Who owns the Framework and updates it?
faqs.a: Head of AI & Automation owns it. Updates require Council consensus. Annual review scheduled Q1.

faqs.q: What happens if someone bypasses governance?
faqs.a: Immediate suspension of access + investigation. Escalation to leadership. Training required before reinstatement. Repeated violations: disciplinary action.

faqs.q: Where does this fit with SDLC 2.0?
faqs.a: SDLC 2.0 is the overall strategy. This Framework is the operational how-to: roles, meetings, decisions, escalations.

docs.title: AI Control Register
docs.tl_dr: Master list of 40+ controls across 9 domains (Data, Model, Security, Testing, Monitoring, Ethical Use, Change, Third-Party, Audit). Maps each control to tier (which tiers require it), regulatory refs, and owner. Live register; updated quarterly. Basis for control testing and audit.

faqs.q: How many controls are in the register?
faqs.a: 42 controls across 9 domains. Tier-1: 8 baseline controls. Tier-2: +12. Tier-3: +22 (full set). Data domain has most controls (9); Ethical Use has fewest (3).

faqs.q: What are the 9 control domains?
faqs.a: Data Governance, Model Governance, Security & Privacy, Testing & QA, Monitoring & Incident Response, Ethical Use, Change Management, Third-Party Risk, Audit & Compliance.

faqs.q: How do I find which controls apply to my project?
faqs.a: Look up your tier in the register. Tier-1 controls are baseline for all projects. Tier-2 adds model and monitoring controls. Tier-3 includes all.

faqs.q: How is control ownership determined?
faqs.a: Data controls: Head of Data. Model controls: Head of AI & Automation. Security: CISO. Testing: Head of QA. Monitoring: DevOps. Audit: CFO office.

faqs.q: What's the audit schedule for controls?
faqs.a: Tier-1: Annual (Q4). Tier-2: Semi-annual (Q2, Q4). Tier-3: Quarterly (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4). Risk team owns audit plan.

faqs.q: If I'm non-compliant with a control, what happens?
faqs.a: Risk team flags as yellow (90-day remediation plan). If not remediated, escalates to red and blocks new project approvals until fixed.

faqs.q: Can controls be waived?
faqs.a: Only by Head of AI & Automation + CRO + CTO joint approval. Waivers are time-bound (max 90 days) and must be documented with risk acceptance.

faqs.q: How often is the register updated?
faqs.a: Quarterly review (scheduled Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4). Emergency updates if new regulatory requirement or critical incident. All changes logged with effective date.

faqs.q: Where can I see the current status of each control?
faqs.a: Live control dashboard on the Intelligence Hub. Shows % implementation, owner, last audit date, and risk status (green/yellow/red).

faqs.q: What's the relationship between Control Register and SDLC 2.0?
faqs.a: SDLC 2.0 is the governance framework. Control Register is the list of specific requirements mapped to tiers. Together: framework + detailed controls.

docs.title: AI Monitoring & Incident Playbook
docs.tl_dr: Procedures for detecting, responding to, and learning from AI incidents: defines severity levels, escalation paths, notification templates, and post-incident reviews. Applies to model drift, data quality issues, security events, and performance degradation. Commits to 15-minute incident response SLA.

faqs.q: What qualifies as an incident?
faqs.a: Severity 1 (Critical): Model accuracy drop >10%, data breach, unplanned outage, security event. Severity 2 (High): Drift >5%, SLA violation, audit finding. Severity 3 (Low): Minor bug, forecast miss, warning log spike.

faqs.q: What's the response SLA?
faqs.a: Severity 1: 15 min ack, incident commander assigned. Severity 2: 1 hour. Severity 3: 8 hours. Timers start when alert fires.

faqs.q: Who do I call first?
faqs.a: Severity 1: Page on-call incident commander + CTO. Severity 2: Slack #incidents + on-call. Severity 3: Log to Jira, no page required.

faqs.q: What monitoring is in place?
faqs.a: Model accuracy (hourly), data quality (real-time), latency (p99, p95), drift detectors (daily), security events (real-time), cost/usage (hourly).

faqs.q: What's the post-incident review process?
faqs.a: Hold within 24h of resolution. Incident commander, responders, stakeholders attend. Document root cause, action items, owner, deadline. Publish to all staff.

faqs.q: Who owns incident tracking and metrics?
faqs.a: DevOps owns on-call schedule and alerts. Head of AI & Automation owns playbook and PIR process. CTO reviews monthly incident summary.

faqs.q: What are common incident causes and fixes?
faqs.a: Model drift: retrain or rollback model. Data quality: check upstream pipeline, investigate anomalies. Performance: scale infra or optimize queries. Security: rotate credentials, audit logs.

faqs.q: Can I trigger a false alert to test the playbook?
faqs.a: Yes. Coordinate with on-call (do not page). Test announced in #incidents 24h in advance. Counts as training, not an incident.

faqs.q: What's the remediation SLA for action items?
faqs.a: Critical actions: 7 days. High: 30 days. Low: 90 days. Review every week in team syncs.

docs.title: Use-Case Intake Form + Tier Scoring Rubric
docs.tl_dr: Intake form and tier-scoring rubric: submit project name, use case, data inputs, expected value, and risk factors. Rubric scores automatically; output is your tier (1, 2, or 3). Baseline for governance gate. Reusable for every new project.

faqs.q: What information must I provide in the intake form?
faqs.a: Project name, team, problem statement, Claude/AI application, input data types, output users, business value ($), timeline, tech stack, risk factors (data sensitivity, regulation, precedent).

faqs.q: How long does intake take to complete?
faqs.a: Typically 30 minutes for experienced teams. Form auto-saves. Required fields: ~15. Optional fields: ~10. Guidance text throughout.

faqs.q: What's the tier rubric?
faqs.a: Four dimensions scored 1-5: Business Impact (revenue, customer scope), Data Sensitivity (PII, regulation), Technical Risk (novel model, unproven tech), Precedent (similar approved projects). Total score determines tier.

faqs.q: What scores map to tiers?
faqs.a: Tier 1: Total 4-8. Tier 2: 9-15. Tier 3: 16+. Tied edge case: manual Council review. Each dimension must be ≥1 to have valid score.

faqs.q: Can I dispute my tier?
faqs.a: Yes. Request manual Council review if you believe rubric mis-scored. Council review required for all edge cases (tied scores, ambiguous data). Include rationale.

faqs.q: Who reviews my intake?
faqs.a: Tier-1: Governance analyst (auto-approval). Tier-2: AI Council vote. Tier-3: Council + legal + board. Average review time: 2-10 days depending on tier.

faqs.q: Can I start work before approval?
faqs.a: Tier-1: scoping is OK; no code/data work. Tier-2 & 3: must wait. Violations block project approval and require executive escalation.

faqs.q: How do I resubmit if my tier escalates?
faqs.a: Same intake form, update changed fields (data, scope, value, risk). Governance analyst flags as resubmission. Retriggers review cycle.

faqs.q: Is the form the same for all projects?
faqs.a: Yes. One form for all Claude/AI use cases. Custom variants (if any) approved by Head of AI & Automation.

faqs.q: Where do I find the intake form?
faqs.a: Intelligence Hub > AI Governance > Use Case Intake. Also via direct link and email to governance@[company].

docs.title: AI Vendor & Third-Party DDQ
docs.tl_dr: Due diligence questionnaire for vendors offering AI/Claude tooling: covers data handling, security, SLAs, compliance certs, incident response, pricing. Use before signing contract. Ensures vendor meets org standards.

faqs.q: When do I use this DDQ?
faqs.a: Any vendor proposing AI tools, services, or integrations. Use early (before commercial negotiation). Shared with vendor via secure portal.

faqs.q: How many questions are in the DDQ?
faqs.a: 35 questions across 8 sections: Data Security, Compliance, SLAs, Incident Response, Pricing/Commercial, Support, Integration, Roadmap.

faqs.q: Who completes the DDQ?
faqs.a: Vendor (required). Scoring and assessment by Procurement + Engineering + Risk. Red-flag answers escalated to legal.

faqs.q: What makes a vendor fail the DDQ?
faqs.a: Critical fails: no encryption in transit/rest, no incident SLA, SOC 2 missing, no DPA, retention >90 days. Fail blocks evaluation; vendor must remediate.

faqs.q: How long is the DDQ process?
faqs.a: Vendor response: 2 weeks (typical). Scoring: 1 week. Remediation/negotiation: 2-4 weeks. Total: 4-7 weeks.

faqs.q: Can I waive DDQ requirements?
faqs.a: Only with Risk + Legal approval. Waivers require documented risk acceptance and are time-bound (12 months max).

faqs.q: Is the DDQ the same for all vendors?
faqs.a: Mostly. Customized sections for different vendor types (SaaS vs. on-prem vs. consulting). Framework is standard.

faqs.q: Who owns vendor relationships post-DDQ?
faqs.a: Procurement (SLA, pricing, renewals). Engineering (technical integration, support). Risk (ongoing compliance, audits).

docs.title: Vendor AI Tools SOW Addendum
docs.tl_dr: Contract addendum for vendor AI tools: adds data handling, IP ownership, liability limits, audit rights, breach notification, and indemnity clauses. Must be attached to all AI vendor SOWs. Protects org from data and IP risk.

faqs.q: When must I use this addendum?
faqs.a: Any new vendor AI/automation service. Existing contracts: use for renewals. Must be signed before vendor access to our data.

faqs.q: What sections does the addendum cover?
faqs.a: Data Protection (classification, encryption, retention, deletion), IP Ownership, Liability & Indemnity, Audit Rights, Breach Notification, Compliance Certs, SLAs, Support & Escalation.

faqs.q: Can a vendor modify the addendum terms?
faqs.a: Negotiation is expected. Red lines (no-trade): data must be encrypted; we retain IP; 24h breach notification; audit rights. Lower-priority items (SLA level, support hours) are negotiable.

faqs.q: Who signs the addendum?
faqs.a: Both parties sign. Vendor signatory must have authority. Legal review required before signature.

faqs.q: What happens if vendor data is breached?
faqs.a: Vendor notifies us within 24h. Vendor owns investigation and notification to regulators (if required). We handle customer notification. Vendor bears costs + indemnifies us.

faqs.q: How long can vendor retain our data?
faqs.a: No longer than necessary to provide service. Default: 30 days. Extended retention (e.g., for backups) requires documented need and encryption.

faqs.q: Does vendor have audit rights too?
faqs.a: No. Only we audit them. Symmetric right is not in scope. Vendor can request attestation (SOC 2) instead.

faqs.q: Who owns intellectual property created by the service?
faqs.a: We own all IP (models, outputs, derivatives). Vendor retains rights to their platform/framework. Clearly separated in addendum.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot Rollout Plan
docs.tl_dr: Three-phase rollout (Pilot Q2, Expansion Q3, Scale Q4): seat provisioning, IDE setup, training, and adoption metrics. Targets 50 pilot, 120 full rollout. Commits to daily DAU tracking and weekly steering.

faqs.q: What's the rollout plan?
faqs.a: Phase 1 (Q2 weeks 4-8): 50 pilot users, daily standup, weekly feedback. Phase 2 (Q3): 120 users (all engineers), office hours, community. Phase 3 (Q4): org-wide, SME program.

faqs.q: How do I get Copilot?
faqs.a: Phase 1: Opt-in survey, selected from volunteers. Phase 2: Auto-provisioned as part of onboarding. Phase 3: All engineers get seat.

faqs.q: What IDEs are supported?
faqs.a: VS Code (primary), JetBrains suite (IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand), Neovim (beta). Other IDEs: contact DevOps for status.

faqs.q: How do I install Copilot?
faqs.a: VS Code: install extension, authenticate with GitHub Enterprise. JetBrains: same flow via IDE plugin. Automated provisioning for Phase 2+.

faqs.q: What training is provided?
faqs.a: Phase 1: async video + office hours. Phase 2: lunch-and-learn, best practices guide. Phase 3: advanced workshops (prompt engineering, integration patterns).

faqs.q: How is adoption tracked?
faqs.a: GitHub provides telemetry: daily active users, accept rate (% of completions accepted), usage patterns. Dashboard shared with leadership weekly.

faqs.q: What's the success metric for the pilot?
faqs.a: >30% of pilot users using Copilot at least 3x/week. >25% accept rate. Positive feedback score >4/5.

faqs.q: Can I opt out of Copilot?
faqs.a: Phase 1 & 2: yes, opt-out via IT. Phase 3: tentative (TBD by leadership). Privacy controls: code retention set to none (no training).

faqs.q: Who owns the rollout?
faqs.a: Head of Engineering (sponsor). DevOps (provisioning). Head of AI & Automation (governance & training). Team leads (adoption, feedback).

faqs.q: What if Copilot doesn't meet expectations?
faqs.a: Go/no-go decision at end of Phase 1 (week 8). If <30% adoption or major issues, escalate to CTO. Possible pivot to alternative tools or extended pilot.

docs.title: AI Sandbox Reference Architecture
docs.tl_dr: Infrastructure blueprint for AI sandbox environment: isolated network, restricted API access, data masking, monitoring, and audit logging. Use for safe Tier-2 & 3 experiments. Reduces security risk of Claude integration.

faqs.q: What is the AI sandbox?
faqs.a: Isolated infrastructure environment for experimenting with Claude models without exposing production data or systems. Used for POCs, testing, and development.

faqs.q: Who should use the sandbox?
faqs.a: Teams running Tier-2 or Tier-3 AI use cases. Tier-1 teams can use sandbox optionally for extra safety.

faqs.q: What's included in the reference architecture?
faqs.a: VPC (isolated network), API gateway (restricted access to Claude), RDS (masked data), monitoring (CloudWatch), logging (audit trail), secret management (KMS), and disaster recovery.

faqs.q: How do I request a sandbox?
faqs.a: Contact DevOps + provide: project name, expected data volume, team members needing access. Provisioning: 1-2 weeks. Includes onboarding.

faqs.q: Can I move data from sandbox to production?
faqs.a: Yes, once use case is approved (Tier-2+). Data migration must include: validation, audit logging, and sign-off by data owner.

faqs.q: How is data masked in the sandbox?
faqs.a: PII redacted (customer names, IDs), numeric fields shifted, text anonymized. Preserves data distribution for realistic testing. Configurable per use case.

faqs.q: How long can I keep a sandbox running?
faqs.a: Tier-2 pilot phase: 12 weeks (renewable). Tier-3: depends on stage (approved for production migration). Idle sandboxes shut down after 60 days inactivity.

faqs.q: Who owns sandbox infrastructure?
faqs.a: DevOps owns provisioning and maintenance. Engineering team owns data and security controls within sandbox.

faqs.q: What happens to my sandbox data after I'm done?
faqs.a: Automatic deletion 30 days after sandbox termination. Option to archive (encrypted) for 90 days if needed for audit.

docs.title: Vendor AI Acceleration Playbook
docs.tl_dr: Step-by-step playbook for acquiring and integrating vendor AI tools (Anthropic Claude API, OpenAI, etc.): DDQ, negotiation, contract, integration, testing, monitoring. Shortens procurement from 12 weeks to 4 weeks.

faqs.q: What does the playbook cover?
faqs.a: Discovery & evaluation, DDQ issuance, commercial negotiation, SOW addendum, technical integration, testing (security, performance), production launch, monitoring.

faqs.q: How long does a vendor integration take?
faqs.a: Fast-track (playbook): 4 weeks. Traditional (ad-hoc): 12 weeks. Acceleration = parallel workstreams + pre-approved templates.

faqs.q: Who are the key stakeholders?
faqs.a: Product (use case definition), Engineering (technical feasibility), Procurement (vendor negotiation), Finance (licensing), Risk (security review), Legal (contract).

faqs.q: What's the procurement workflow?
faqs.a: Week 1: DDQ (parallel with eval). Week 2: Negotiation (pricing, terms, SLA). Week 3: Legal & signing. Week 4: Integration & testing. Week 5 (if needed): remediation.

faqs.q: Do all vendors go through the same process?
faqs.a: Core path is standard (DDQ, SOW, testing). Fast-track available for pre-approved vendors (Anthropic, OpenAI) if budget <$100K/year.

faqs.q: What's the minimum viable contract?
faqs.a: SOW + Addendum (data handling, IP, audit, breach, liability). Must include: data encryption, 30-day retention, 24h breach notification, audit rights, indemnity.

faqs.q: Who approves vendor selection?
faqs.a: Product + Engineering (technical fit). Procurement (commercial). Risk + Legal (security/legal). CFO (budget >$100K). CTO (strategic tech decisions).

faqs.q: What testing is required before production?
faqs.a: Security (pen test, credential handling), performance (latency, throughput), reliability (failover, backup), compliance (audit readiness).

faqs.q: How do I estimate vendor costs?
faqs.a: API-based: per-token or per-API-call pricing. License-based: per-seat or annual. Include: support, training, implementation. Negotiate volume discounts if >$500K/year.

docs.title: Intelligent Test Automation Strategy
docs.tl_dr: Document covers key concepts and processes related to AI governance and operations.

faqs.q: What is the Intelligent Test Automation Strategy?
faqs.a: Use Claude to auto-generate test cases, assertions, and test maintenance for unit and integration tests. Pilot on 1-2 products to measure velocity and coverage improvements. Goal: reduce test maintenance by 20% within 12 months.

faqs.q: What types of tests can Claude generate?
faqs.a: Unit tests (primary use case), integration tests, and API tests. GUI and end-to-end testing are lower priority but possible. Focus is on reducing manual test writing and assertion maintenance.

faqs.q: How much faster is test generation with Claude?
faqs.a: Typical speedup: 3-5x faster test creation. Maintenance (updating assertions after code changes) is also ~3x faster. Conservative estimate for overall test productivity gain: 20%.

faqs.q: Which products are participating in the pilot?
faqs.a: TBD. Selection criteria: high test coverage baseline, active development, clear success metrics (coverage percentage, maintenance hours). Pilot targets 1-2 products in Q2-Q3.

faqs.q: How is test quality ensured?
faqs.a: AI-generated tests are reviewed by engineers before commit. Assertion logic is validated manually. Edge cases are tested. Coverage metrics tracked weekly in CI/CD.

faqs.q: What tools will be used for test generation?
faqs.a: Three options being evaluated: 1) GitHub Copilot inline IDE suggestions, 2) CLI tool for batch test generation, 3) Foundry fine-tuned Claude model for domain-specific test patterns.

faqs.q: How is success measured?
faqs.a: Baseline coverage pre-pilot. Measure weekly: test creation time, maintenance hours, coverage %. Target: maintain ≥80% coverage while reducing test maintenance by 20%.

faqs.q: Who owns the test automation strategy?
faqs.a: Head of QA (strategy ownership). Engineering teams (implementation, validation). Head of AI & Automation (governance, Copilot integration). Decision-making by these three parties.

faqs.q: When is the go/no-go decision on full rollout?
faqs.a: End of Q3 pilot. If >20% productivity gain measured, roll out to all products. If <10% gain, strategy pauses for reassessment. All decisions documented.

faqs.q: Is test automation subject to AI governance?
faqs.a: Yes. Test automation is classified as a Tier-2 use case (internal, medium impact). Pilot requires AI Council review via use case intake. Full rollout may remain Tier-2 or move to Tier-1 based on governance review.

docs.title: Spark — Continental Innovation Challenge · Rules & Judging Charter
docs.tl_dr: Governing charter for the Spark Continental Innovation Challenge — the quarterly $100K competition where staff across all 13 Opcos submit ideas, vote, and see the top three funded as pilots. Defines eligibility, submission + voting rules, a weighted 60/40 panel-plus-community scoring model, and a tiered prize pool of $50K/$25K/$15K with a further $10K across honourable mentions. Ratified by the AI Council, v1.0, effective 24 April 2026.
key_audiences: AI Council members and judging panel
Group Legal, Risk, and HR (for compliance, IP, conflicts)
Finance and Group Tax (prize payout treatment)

faqs.q: Who can submit ideas to Spark?
faqs.a: All permanent and fixed-term staff employed by a Group entity or a participating Opco are eligible. Contractors on engagements of three months or longer are eligible with their sponsoring manager's written consent. Judges, Council members during their term, interns under three months' tenure, and staff on active PIPs or disciplinary process are not eligible. Third parties (vendors, consultancies) cannot submit but can be cited in support.

faqs.q: How many ideas can I submit and can I co-author?
faqs.a: Each staff member may submit up to three ideas per quarterly round. Joint submissions of up to three co-authors are permitted — the lead author receives any prize allocation, with an obligation to share with co-authors per the team's own agreement.

faqs.q: How does voting work and can I vote for my own idea?
faqs.a: Every eligible staff member gets a fixed pool of 20 votes per round, distributable across any number of ideas (up to 3 per single idea). Self-voting is prohibited — you cannot vote for your own ideas, your co-authored ideas, or ideas authored by your direct manager. Vote-campaigning is allowed at reasonable one-to-many scale but quid-pro-quo offers, coordinated bloc voting, or a manager directing their team's votes results in nullification and potential disqualification.

faqs.q: How are winners actually chosen — is it just vote count?
faqs.a: No. Shortlist selection and pilot funding use a weighted scoring rubric applied by a judging panel chaired by the Head of AI & Automation. Five dimensions are scored 1–5: customer/business impact (30%), feasibility (20%), strategic alignment (20%), originality (15%), and risk & governance (15%). The weighted panel score is combined 60/40 with the community vote count (normalised 0–100) to produce the final pilot-funding score.

faqs.q: What are the five pipeline stages an idea moves through?
faqs.a: Submitted (idea filed; passes automated AI review) → Voted (live for community voting, typically 3 weeks) → Shortlist (top 20 by combined score advance to clarification interviews) → Pilot (Council-approved funding, with named sponsor, lead, success criteria, and 90-day scope) → Scaled (pilot meets success criteria; promoted to Active Projects portfolio).

faqs.q: What's the timeline — when are ideas due and when are winners announced?
faqs.a: Spark runs on a quarterly cadence with four rounds per year aligned to the Group financial calendar. Each round is thirteen weeks: weeks 1–3 open submissions, weeks 4–6 community voting, week 7 shortlist published, weeks 8–9 panel scoring and clarification interviews, week 10 winners announced, weeks 11–13 pilot kickoffs. One flagship round per year (typically Q3) runs an extended five-week voting window and carries an enhanced prize pool.

faqs.q: How is the $100,000 prize pool split?
faqs.a: Tiered by place: $50,000 to the 1st place winner, $25,000 to 2nd place, $15,000 to 3rd place, and a $10,000 pool split equally across 4th–10th place honourable mentions (approximately $1,430 each). Prizes are paid within 60 days of announcement through Opco payroll, subject to local tax withholding. Group Tax publishes a per-country note each round.

faqs.q: Is prize money the same as pilot funding?
faqs.a: No — they are separate and independent allocations. Prize money goes to the lead author as a one-time bonus. Pilot funding is a separate allocation made by the AI Council to actually build the winning idea. Pilot funding may be clawed back if a pilot is cancelled for cause; prize money may not.

faqs.q: Who owns the IP on a submitted idea?
faqs.a: All ideas submitted to Spark are the intellectual property of the Group. By submitting, staff grant the Group a perpetual, royalty-free, worldwide licence to implement, modify, and commercialise the idea — aligning with the standard employment contract of each participating entity. Submissions are internal-confidential through the Voted stage and internal-all-staff from Shortlist onward.

faqs.q: Can I include real customer data in an idea submission?
faqs.a: No. Submissions must not contain personally identifiable customer data (use synthetic or aggregated examples), third-party trade secrets, material non-public information about the Group or any Opco, or data subject to contractual confidentiality obligations. Ideas involving personal data processing must comply with the Group Data Protection Policy and cannot progress past Shortlist without a completed data protection pre-assessment.

faqs.q: What counts as a conflict of interest and how is it handled?
faqs.a: Judges, Council members, and managers involved in scoring must declare any actual, potential, or perceived conflict of interest before scoring begins — including close personal relationships with an author, prior commercial relationships with a named vendor, and any pre-existing financial interest in the idea's domain. Recusal is automatic where declared.
faqs.section: 10. Conflicts of Interest & Code of Conduct

faqs.q: If I think the rules have been breached, how do I raise a dispute?
faqs.a: Raise a dispute within 72 hours of the event through the Spark section of the Hub or by email to spark-appeals@group. Disputes are triaged by the Head of AI & Automation and, if substantiated, heard by a three-person Council panel (excluding members with a conflict). The panel commits to a decision within ten working days. Remedies include vote nullification, disqualification, re-opening a stage, or no action.

faqs.q: Who owns this charter and how can it be changed?
faqs.a: The charter is owned and ratified by the AI Council. It is reviewed annually and amendments may be issued between reviews where operational reality requires it. Material changes — to prize mechanics, judging weights, or eligibility — require a simple majority of the Council plus advance notice of at least one round. Current version is v1.0, effective 24 April 2026; change history is maintained in the Group document store and is visible to all staff.
